issues.legal_issue: An estate agent authorised to negotiate a property sale and secure a buyer is not authorised to conclude a binding sale contract unless the principal’s instructions clearly confer that authority.
material_facts: The principal authorised an estate agent in writing to negotiate the sale of property and stated a minimum price, that the property would be free from encumbrances, and that good title would be made out.
The instructions did not specify important terms of the sale, including payment, investigation and approval of title, conveyance, and related costs.
The agent exchanged letters with prospective buyers purporting to conclude a sale contract, but the courts found that the agent lacked authority to bind the principal to that contract.
issues.conclusion: The commission note did not authorise the agent to conclude a binding contract of sale on the principal’s behalf.
issues.legal_principle: An estate agent’s authority to negotiate a sale or find a purchaser does not, without clear words, include authority to bind the owner to a sale contract. The court relied on Chadburn v. Moore (67 L.T. 257), Rosenbaum v. Belson ([1900] 2 Ch. 267), and Durga Charan Mitra v. Rajendra Narayan Sinha (36 C.L.J. 467), and distinguished authority to negotiate from authority to conclude a sale. The court also noted that the detailed terms ordinarily required for a transfer of real property support this distinction.

predicates.estate_sale_agency_case: The dispute concerns an agent engaged to arrange the sale of real property for a principal.
predicates.instructions_authorise_negotiation_or_bu: The principal instructed the agent to negotiate a sale or find a buyer.
predicates.instructions_clearly_authorise_binding_s: The principal expressly authorised the agent to conclude a binding sale contract on the principal’s behalf.
predicates.material_sale_terms_left_for_later_agree: Important terms of the property sale were not settled in the instructions and remained for later agreement between the principal and buyer.

issues.definition: When an estate agent is instructed to negotiate or find a buyer, but is not clearly authorised to bind the principal and important sale terms remain unsettled, the agent lacks authority to bind the principal to the sale.

issues.legal_issue: An agent who secures a firm offer at a stated price earns commission calculated on that price when the principal later completes the sale with the buyers introduced by the agent, even if the principal completes at a lower price.
material_facts: The agent secured two prospective buyers who made a firm offer at a price above the minimum specified by the principal.
The principal later sold the property to those buyers, through their nominee, at a lower price than the firm offer.
The courts found that the later sale was the direct result of the agent’s efforts.
The commission agreement provided remuneration by reference to the price secured by the agent.
issues.conclusion: The agent was entitled to commission calculated on the price of the firm offer he had secured, notwithstanding that the principal completed the sale to the introduced buyers at a lower price.
issues.legal_principle: Where the principal completes the transaction with the buyer introduced by the agent, the event giving rise to commission has occurred and the agent’s right to commission becomes vested; the principal cannot reduce that right by completing the sale at a lower price. The court distinguished Luxor (Eastbourne) Ltd. v. Cooper ([1941] A.C. 108): a commission right contingent on completion becomes vested when the transaction is completed with the introduced buyer. It also relied on the finding that the agent’s efforts were the effective cause of the sale.
